explanation: A viewing page can hide an empty folder or tab, collapse filter details, or omit a field on a specialized empty-state screen while keeping the saved configuration intact. This pattern matches a report that treats that absence from the viewing layout as deletion, even though reopening the editor, expanding the controls or adding content reveals the retained setting. Confirm the owning settings and applied behavior before claiming storage loss. The fact that data is intact does not by itself decide whether a separate promised display behavior is broken.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in as fixture administrator eval and set the browser viewport to 390×844 CSS pixels. Create a uniquely named private repository owned by eval. Enter Mobile repository description verification as the description, leaving template and initialization unchecked. Inspect the resulting empty repository homepage, scroll through its Quick Guide, and refresh. The entered description is absent from the visible page body. As controls, open Repository Settings and the owner profile repository listing to confirm that the description was saved. After a first commit through New File, the normal repository homepage displays it at mobile and desktop widths. The rejected report expected: The newly created repository page displays “Mobile repository description verification.”. It claimed this outcome: At 390×844, the created repository showed its name and Quick Guide, but not the entered description anywhere in the page. The omission remained after scrolling through the page and refreshing. Review concluded: The user explicitly rejected this as intentional empty-repository presentation. The omission is real, but the saved description remains visible in Settings, the owner profile listing and the browser title; after the first commit, the repository homepage displays it normally. Empty repositories use a separate Quick Guide template. This records the human acceptance of that presentation, rather than claiming the original observation is false or that a maintainer explicitly required the omission. Desktop repetition alone does not invalidate the mobile observation.

explanation: A report's specific factual claim is contradicted by a decisive observation or by a controlled repetition of the same setup. For example, the allegedly deleted value is still present, or the allegedly broken control performs the requested action when activated as described. Match this pattern only when that counterevidence addresses the same value, action and conditions; a vaguely similar successful workflow is insufficient. The finding rejects the checked allegation, not every related defect or every possible historical failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Using the provided authenticated session, start signed in as the admin account at /admin/harbor-handbook. Open the top-navigation create menu (+) and choose New Repository. Create a fresh private repository owned by admin named management-branch-approval-qa-6d9c, with Initialize Repository checked so it has a README and main branch. In the new repository, open Settings > Branches > Add New Rule. Set Protected Branch Name Pattern to main, leave Required approvals at its default 0, then save the rule. Click Edit for the main branch protection rule. Change Required approvals to 1 and click Save Rule. Observe the success banner stating that branch protection for rule main has been updated. Reopen Edit for main and inspect Required approvals; it shows 0. As a falsification check, set Required approvals to 1 and save once more, then reopen Edit for main. The success banner appears again, and Required approvals again shows 0. The rejected report expected: After saving Required approvals as 1, reopening the main branch protection rule should show 1. The UI labels the setting Required approvals and says it limits merges to pull requests with enough approvals; the success banner says the rule was updated. It claimed this outcome: The rule edit form showed 1 before saving and the page displayed “Branch protection for rule "main" has been updated.” Reopening Edit showed Required approvals as 0. Repeating the save and reopen produced the same result. Review concluded: User-approved rejection after pinned-source review. The Required approvals form binds required_approvals, the handler assigns the submitted value directly, AllCols persists it, and reopening renders the stored value. The normal successful save of 1 does not silently persist 0 as claimed.

explanation: An approval can be judged under the eligibility rules in effect when it was given. This pattern matches a report that tightens a rule afterward, such as changing an allowed approver list or team membership, and assumes every previously valid approval must be invalidated automatically. Review accepted checking those approvals at approval time. An ineligible new approval being accepted, or an old approval being carried onto a different protected target, needs separate analysis.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Protect a branch with 1 required approval, then have a collaborator approve a PR into it. Edit the protection rule: enable the approval allowlist without that collaborator and save. Return to the PR and check the approval count and whether it can be merged. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that approvals count toward required approvals only if the reviewer is on the current approval allowlist when the merge is evaluated. It claimed this outcome: With one required approval, a reviewer approved and then the allowlist was changed to exclude them. Their earlier approval still satisfied the requirement and the PR merged, including with an empty allowlist. A fresh approval from the same reviewer under the restricted rule showed 0 of 1, 'Uncounted approval'. Review concluded: User-rejected. Applying a tightened approval allowlist only to approvals given after the change is an acceptable design: an approval that was valid under the rule in force when it was given keeps counting. The upstream fix for re-evaluating approvals on retarget (go-gitea/gitea#38319) covers moving an already-approved PR onto a protected branch, which is a different case.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Protect a branch to require one approval from a specific team. Have a team member approve a pull request. Remove that user from the team. Check whether the pull request can still be merged. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that removing the approver from the allowlisted team withdraws their approval's effect, so the pull request isn't mergeable. It claimed this outcome: After the approving user was removed from the Reviewers team (0 members), the pull request still showed as ready and merged using that earlier approval. Review concluded: Intended per the existing ruling: an approval is checked against the allowlist when it's given, and later allowlist or team changes don't retroactively remove it. Same reasoning as the rejected 'Restricting the approval allowlist doesn't stop earlier approvals from counting'; this entry is the reviewer being removed from the team.

explanation: An input can visibly change unsupported characters, dates or numeric precision while the user is still editing. This pattern matches a report that remembers the intended text and blames Save for a different result, although the field or preview already displayed that effective value before submission and the save preserved it. Observe the value immediately before saving and compare it with storage. A valid displayed value secretly replaced only during submission is a different failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open New Repository. Enter a repository name containing a slash, such as qa/name, and move focus out of the field. Create the repository and check its name. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that a name with a slash is rejected with a validation message instead of being changed. It claimed this outcome: Entering 'qa-creation/m7x91' as the repository name created eval/qa-creation-m7x91 with no warning. Review concluded: Intended: Gitea deliberately sanitizes repository names in the browser when the name field loses focus, turning characters such as '/' into '-' (go-gitea/gitea#33986, 'Sanitize repo name for migration and new repo', with a unit test expecting this). The change is visible in the field before submitting, so it isn't silent, and a name that skips the cleanup is still rejected by the server's validation.

explanation: A focused numeric input can increase or decrease when the mouse wheel scrolls over it. This pattern matches a report that remembers the earlier typed number, overlooks the visibly changed draft, and blames Save or refresh for the decrement even though the displayed submitted value is preserved. Check the field immediately before Save and repeat while scrolling outside it. A number first changing during submission, without a prior input interaction, is outside this rejection.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open a branch protection rule in repository Settings > Branches. Enter 0 in Required approvals. Click Save Rule. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that 0 required approvals saves successfully. It claimed this outcome: After entering 0 in Required approvals and clicking Save Rule, the editor showed 'Required approvals cannot be negative.' and the rule wasn't saved. Review concluded: Not reproduced: 0 required approvals saves fine in repeated attempts on desktop and mobile; only negative values are rejected, as the message says. In the report, the page was scrolled with the mouse wheel while the focused number field still held 0, which steps a number input's value down below 0 before Save Rule was clicked, so the submitted value really was negative.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open a branch protection rule in repository Settings > Branches. Enter 2147483648 in Required approvals and click Save Rule. Reopen the rule and check the value. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the rule reopens with the entered 2147483648. It claimed this outcome: After entering 2147483648 in Required approvals and saving, reopening the rule was reported to show 2147483647. Review concluded: Not reproduced: 2147483648 saves and reopens as 2147483648; the value is stored as a 64-bit integer throughout. In the report, the page was scrolled with the mouse wheel while the focused number field held 2147483648, which steps a number input's value down by one before Save Rule was clicked, so 2147483647 is what was actually submitted.

explanation: Markup is source text interpreted into formatted output, so the displayed result need not reproduce every source character or line break literally. In the reviewed cases, ordinary Markdown line breaks were rendered as soft breaks, or restricted HTML was interpreted and sanitized while the saved source remained intact. This pattern matches a claim of text loss based only on that supported rendering behavior. Compare the saved source with the markup rules; actual stored-text deletion or incorrectly rendered supported syntax is a different failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: In repository Settings, set the description to text that includes '<test>' and save. Reload Settings and confirm the full text is kept. Open the Code page and read the description in the sidebar. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the Code page shows the description exactly as entered, including '<test>'. It claimed this outcome: With the description 'QA updated description — café & <test>' saved in Settings, the Code page sidebar showed 'QA updated description — café &'. Review concluded: Intended: repository descriptions are rendered as restricted HTML, so tags outside a small allowed list are removed from the display, and '<test>' is treated as an unknown tag (the description sanitizer and its unit test assert this). The saved description is unchanged, as the Settings form shows, and the same text without angle brackets displays in full.

explanation: A resource’s default private visibility can coexist with an explicit permission granting broader access to selected sections. This pattern matches a report that configures such a grant, observes exactly the granted access and calls it a privacy bypass because the person is not otherwise a collaborator. Check the setting’s stated audience and whether removing the grant removes access. Access to an ungranted section, access by someone outside the configured audience, or a separate inconsistent API response requires its own assessment.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, create a private repository and explicitly set Code and Issues to Everyone Read in Settings > Public Access. A signed-in person who is not a collaborator can now read those configured sections, and resetting them to Not set removes that access. Review rejected the claim that private visibility must override this explicit grant: Everyone Read intentionally grants all signed-in users access to the selected section. This rejection does not grade the separate repository-details API 403 response.
